text:
Illinois needs a second high school athletic association and not because the IHSA needs to disappear.

Before going any further, let me stress this: We should all be thankful for the IHSA, its leadership and the 1,000s of people who have worked - and continue working - tirelessly to create opportunities for kids, families, schools and communities.

They've done, and continue to do, a tremendous amount of good.

But one association cannot be everything to every school and every student athlete in a state as large and diverse as Illinois.

People deserve choices.

Professional sports, college sports and youth sports all have different competitive platforms. Even education offers different pathways in the classroom.

But high school sports in Illinois? One association, one system and one outdated model that has ended up in court and with state legislators quite a bit the last five years.  

Think about the 100s of Illinois high schools competing in a system where many of the same programs dominate year after year. 

How many schools go five, 10 or even 20 years without meaningful postseason success? How many student athletes enter postseason competition knowing they’re significantly overmatched before the opening whistle?

Seriously, think about the 100s of schools and 1,000s of kids that do.

So tell me again: Why is one association the only acceptable model?

Look at Florida, as I pointed out earlier on Thursday.

In 2008, eight schools helped establish the Sunshine State Athletic Association (SSAA), creating an alternative to the traditional state association. The SSAA has since grown into a substantial statewide organization with 160 schools, demonstrating that multiple associations can coexist.

Illinois can - and should - do the same.

Smaller public and private schools and programs that have historically struggled to experience postseason success should help one another. Create competitive divisions based on resources AND actual athletic performance - not simply enrollment.

Here’s a perfect example of why this deserves discussion. Morton High School in Cicero has more than 8,000 students across its district campuses.

Its boys soccer program has been a powerhouse, but what about girls basketball? It hasn’t had a winning season in 10 years.

If a program struggles year after year, should its athletes automatically compete in the largest postseason classification simply because of the school’s enrollment?

Why should success in one sport determine the competitive expectations for another? Why wouldn’t we consider sport-specific performance, competitive history and available resources when building postseason opportunities?

That's not lowering standards. That’s recognizing that competitive balance should be about the actual teams competing, not just the number of students walking through the school doors.

We need to create more meaningful opportunities for kids to compete, advance, improve and experience success.

Kids don’t need more games. They need more experiences. And no dummy, nobody is suggesting every kid deserves a trophy.

You know what every kid does deserve? A legitimate opportunity to compete.

Think about schools such as Thornridge, Illinois Lutheran, Bulls College Prep and West Prairie.

Are their student athletes consistently receiving the competitive postseason opportunities that best serve their development? Could a different postseason structure offer some of these schools something better?

Those are the honest questions school leaders should be asking vs. protecting a system simply because it’s the system we’ve always had.

Competition creates innovation. Choice creates accountability. Opportunity creates participation.

There shouldn’t be any question that Illinois needs a second high school athletic association.

The question is why adult school leaders continue accepting a one-size-fits-all model when they have the power to create something better.

#MoreThanJUSTGames

the snake with a mans face: glycon, alexander and the man who tried to kill a god with a book

Somewhere around the 150s AD, on the Black Sea coast of Paphlagonia (north Turkey now), a little town called Abonoteichus got a god. Not one that evolved over centuries like everybody elses. One that got delivered, practically overnight, by a man named Alexander. The god was Glycon, a great serpent with a face that looked almost human. Within a generation people were worshipping him from the Danube to Rome, his face was on the towns coins, and a Roman senator was married to the prophets daughter. Then a satirist named Lucian wrote a pamphlet that has basically been the only lens anyone ever looked through since.

I want to go through all of it. the man, the god, the enemy, and how far the thing actually reached, because its one of the strangest religious stories of the whole Roman period and its almost never told from anyone but Lucian's side.

the source problem first

Almost everything we know comes from one text, Lucian of Samosata's Alexander or the False Prophet, written around 180 AD, about ten years after Alexander died. Lucian hated him and says so openly. He wrote it as a letter to his Epicurean friend Celsus. (probably not the same Celsus who wrote against the Christians, though people argue about it.) So every detail of the "fraud" comes from a man mocking a living cult and settling a personal score. Keep that in mind, because the archaeology tells a slightly different story. It doesnt say Lucian lied. It says the thing he laughed at was way bigger and lasted way longer than his pamphlet lets on.

alexander of abonoteichus

Lucian says Alexander was tall, handsome, a great talker, long hair, a voice people remembered. As a boy he was apprenticed to a doctor-magician who'd been a student of Apollonius of Tyana, the famous wonder-working Pythagorean. Thats important and people skip it. Alexander came out of the same world of healing, magic and Pythagorean holiness that produced Apollonius. Not a random con man. He was trained in a tradition.

He and a partner, Cocconas, went looking for a place to start an oracle. They passed over the big cities and picked his own hometown, because the Paphlagonians were (in Lucian's snobby words) superstitious and easy to impress. They buried bronze tablets in the temple of Apollo at Chalcedon announcing that Asclepius and his father Apollo were coming to Abonoteichus. The tablets got "discovered," the news spread, and the town voted to build a temple before the god even showed up.

the birth of glycon

The famous part. Alexander hid a newly hatched snake in a hollowed goose egg and sealed it in the mud of the temple foundations. Then he ran into the marketplace half naked, shaking his hair, foaming at the mouth like the old prophets, and led the crowd to the spot. He dug out the egg, cracked it open, and there was the little god. Asclepius born again as a snake.

A few days later the baby was a huge serpent. Lucian says Alexander bought a big tame snake from Pella in Macedonia, where those snakes were so gentle women slept with them and kids played with them. He sat in a dim room with the snake coiled around him. Its real head was tucked under his arm, and a fake head made of linen, painted half human, with a mouth that opened and closed on horsehair strings, stuck out instead. Crowds filed through, got a glimpse in bad light, and were pushed out the other door before anybody could look close. The god was named Glycon, "the sweet one," and announced with a verse: I am Glycon, grandson of Zeus, a light to men.

how the oracle worked

Questions came in on sealed scrolls. Lucian claims Alexander opened them with a hot needle, read them, resealed them and sent back answers, sometimes in verse, sometimes deliberately vague. For more money you got autophones, "self-speaking" oracles where the snake answered out loud. Lucian says that was a tube of crane windpipes running to the linen head, with someone talking into it from the next room.

A drachma and two obols per question. Lucian says Alexander pulled in seventy or eighty thousand a year. He had informers, scribes, interpreters and sealers on staff, and agents abroad spreading the oracles fame and reporting what people were scared of. Thats not just a scam honestly. thats an institution.

the mysteries

Alexander also founded a three day torchlit mystery festival, like Eleusis. It opened with a proclamation driving out the impure, and the crowd shouted "Out with the Christians! Out with the Epicureans!" Day one acted out the birth of Apollo and of Asclepius. Day two, the epiphany of Glycon. Day three, Alexanders own birth and his love affair with Selene the moon, who supposedly fell for him like she fell for Endymion. Lucian says a Roman officials wife played Selene, coming down from the ceiling.

Alexander claimed descent from Podalirius, son of Asclepius. He claimed Pythagoras's soul and flashed a golden thigh at the festival, which is exactly what they said about Pythagoras. So the whole package was a Pythagorean and Asclepian revival around a living holy man and a serpent god. And look at who got banned. Christians and Epicureans, the two groups that denied the gods acted in the world. His real competition, his real enemies.

rome gets involved

The big catch was Publius Mummius Sisenna Rutilianus, a senator and ex-consul who'd governed Moesia and Asia. Lucian calls him a good man in every way except religion. Rutilianus asked the oracle who to marry. Glycon told him to marry Alexanders daughter, whose mother (according to Alexander) was Selene herself. Rutilianus was about sixty and he did it.

Through him the oracle reached the emperor. During the Marcomannic Wars around 170, Marcus Aurelius supposedly followed an oracle of Glycon to throw two live lions into the Danube with spices and sacrifices, and a great victory would follow. The lions swam across, the barbarians clubbed them to death "like dogs or foreign wolves," and the Romans then lost about twenty thousand men. Alexander said the god predicted a victory, just not whose. the classic oracle escape hatch.

During the Antonine plague Glycon gave out a one line verse to hang over your door: Phoebus the long-haired keeps off the cloud of plague. Lucian, being Lucian, says the houses with the verse got hit the worst.

lucian vs alexander

Lucian says he set traps for the oracle, sending sealed questions it couldn't answer. Then he met Alexander in person. Offered the prophets hand to kiss, Lucian bit it, hard. Alexander kept smiling in front of his people, was friendly after, and even lent Lucian a ship home. Lucian says the crew had orders to throw him overboard. The captain refused, cried, and dropped him on the coast. Lucian tried to prosecute and the governor talked him out of it, Alexander was too well connected.

Alexander died at nearly seventy of a gangrenous leg crawling with maggots, which in ancient writing is basically the death you hand impious tyrants. so it means something, its not just medical detail. He'd prophesied he'd live to 150 and die by lightning.

what lucian doesnt tell you: the cult outlived him

Lucian ends it like the fraud died with the fraudster. It didnt.

Coins. Abonoteichus asked the emperor to be renamed Ionopolis, modern İnebolu, and it stuck. Its coins show Glycon, coiled serpent, human-ish head, long hair, from Antoninus Pius to about the mid third century. Thats around a hundred years of official civic worship after Alexander was dead.
The Tomis statue. In 1962 workers in Constanța, Romania (ancient Tomis on the Black Sea) dug up a buried hoard of statues. One is a gorgeous marble Glycon, coiled, with an antelope-like muzzle, human ears and long hair, near life size. Its in the national history museum in Constanța now and its one of the most beautiful religious objects from the whole region. Somebody buried it carefully, probably to save it when things turned against the old gods.
Inscriptions and small finds. Dedications to Glycon turn up in Dacia (Apulum, Romania) and the Danube provinces, especially Moesia, which makes sense since Rutilianus governed there. Theres material from Athens and Asia Minor, and gems and figurines from Rome. Lucian himself says the oracle was consulted from Bithynia, Galatia, Thrace, Italy and Rome.

So the real map: the Paphlagonian coast at the center, around the Black Sea rim (Tomis, Thrace), along the Danube frontier (Moesia, Dacia) where the army was, across Asia Minor, and up into the Roman senate. It followed the roads, the sea lanes and the legions.

the dracon / serpent cult question

People lump this into a bigger "dragon cult," and theres something to that, though not as one secret society. Glycon plugged straight into an old Greek pattern where the healing god comes as a snake, a drakōn. Asclepius came to Athens in 420 BC as a snake (Sophocles supposedly hosted him). He came to Rome in 292 BC as a snake that swam off the ship onto Tiber Island. The tame Pella snakes belong to the same picture. Macedonian legend said Olympias slept with a serpent and that Zeus in snake form fathered Alexander the Great, and I'm pretty sure our Alexander loved sharing that name and used it.

Then theres the agathos daimōn, the good spirit of the house as a bearded snake, and its Egyptian forms. The healing snakes of the Asclepieia, where the sick slept in the temple and snakes licked them in the night. The Gnostic snake groups of the same age, Ophites and Naassenes, who read the Eden serpent as the bringer of knowledge, and the lion-headed Chnoubis serpent on magical gems. Glycon isnt a weird outlier. Hes what happens when all those serpent currents get one man, one town and one festival. Some people tie the long-haired face to Alexanders own long hair, like the god wore the prophets face. The modern chaos magick scene picked up on exactly that (Alan Moore famously worships Glycon, half joking and half not). A god made by a man that then takes on its own life, which is honestly a pretty Neoplatonic problem if you think about it.

what i take from it

Lucian thought he was exposing a puppet. Maybe the head was linen. But a linen head doesnt explain a hundred years of coins, a buried statue in Romania, and soldiers on the Danube leaving offerings. Whatever Alexander started, people kept it going long after the man was gone, because it gave them something. Healing, a god close by, an answer over the door during a plague. Plotinus was alive for the tail end of all this and would've said the image is not the thing, but the soul can still climb by an image if it knows its an image. Thats the line between idolatry and theurgy, and Glycon sits right on it.

Lucian bit the prophets hand. The snake outlived them both.

Representative Buddy Carter’s Efforts to Promote Accountability
Congressman Earl L. “Buddy” Carter of Georgia has also taken legislative action concerning human rights abuses and religious persecution in Ethiopia.
On December 9, 2025, Carter introduced a resolution condemning human rights violations by the Ethiopian government, including persecution of Christians, and urging the U.S. Secretary of State to use available diplomatic and economic tools to protect civilians and hold those responsible for abuses accountable.
The proposed measures included support for independent investigations, protection of religious freedom, and consideration of sanctions and restrictions on foreign assistance where appropriate.
Although the resolution predates the latest October 2026 massacres, its focus on accountability and civilian protection remains relevant to the current crisis.
These congressional efforts demonstrate why continued engagement with members of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate is essential. Lawmakers need accurate information about developments in Ethiopia, and they need to hear from constituents and advocacy organizations calling for practical responses.
Ethiopian Americans have an important role to play in ensuring that these concerns remain on the congressional agenda.
Source: Congressman Buddy Carter’s official announcement on his Ethiopia resolution.
A Continuing Crisis in Arsi
The latest killings did not occur in isolation.
The Arsi Zone has experienced repeated reports of attacks against civilians, including members of Ethiopian Orthodox Christian communities. Reports from the region have described killings, injuries, the destruction of homes, attacks affecting religious institutions, and displacement.
According to the conflict-monitoring organization ACLED, violence targeting civilians in Arsi has included repeated incidents affecting Orthodox Christian residents. Its analysis identifies Shirka as one of the districts particularly affected by this pattern of violence.
The identity of those responsible for individual attacks and the precise circumstances surrounding some incidents remain disputed. Ethiopian regional authorities have blamed armed groups, while other accounts have offered competing allegations. These claims require careful, independent investigation rather than assumptions about responsibility.
What should not be in dispute is the urgent need to protect civilians.
The Ethiopian government and relevant regional authorities must take effective steps to prevent further attacks, investigate reported atrocities impartially, and provide security to communities facing threats.
Credible investigations should establish who planned, carried out, or facilitated the killings and whether any officials failed to meet their legal responsibilities. Those found responsible should face appropriate legal consequences.
Religious institutions and civilian property must also be protected. Churches are not merely buildings; they are sacred places of worship, centers of community life, and important parts of Ethiopia’s historical and cultural heritage.

U.S. Lawmakers Condemn Attacks on Orthodox Christians as Ethiopian Americans Intensify Nationwide Advocacy for Civilian Protection, Justice, and Accountability

By Mesfin Mekonen Washington Update
WASHINGTON, D.C. — October 29, 2026 — The reported massacres of Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians in Ethiopia’s Arsi Zone have renewed concerns about the deteriorating human rights and humanitarian situation in the country and intensified calls for stronger international action to protect civilians.
At least 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in two attacks in the Arsi Zone of the Oromia Regional State on October 20 and October 24, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s Holy Synod. The attacks reportedly occurred in Merti and Shirka districts, where more than 20 additional people sustained serious injuries and approximately 20 homes were burned.
The killings have prompted condemnation from U.S. lawmakers, renewed appeals from religious leaders, and growing calls for the Ethiopian government and international community to take meaningful steps to protect vulnerable communities and ensure accountability for those responsible.
The scale of the reported violence underscores an urgent question: How many more innocent people must die before effective measures are taken to protect civilians and prevent further atrocities?
For Ethiopian Americans and human rights advocates who have spent years calling attention to Ethiopia’s crisis, the latest killings reinforce the importance of sustained advocacy, congressional engagement, independent investigations, and coordinated international pressure.
Congressional Condemnation: A Significant Step Forward
The Republican majority of the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee publicly condemned the continued attacks targeting Christians in Ethiopia, describing the violence as “completely unacceptable.”
The committee’s statement called on all parties to the conflict to protect Christians and people of every faith and to ensure that those responsible for the violence are brought to justice.
This public condemnation represents an important development in efforts to draw greater attention to the suffering of Ethiopian civilians. Congressional statements can help elevate human rights concerns, encourage diplomatic engagement, and communicate that attacks against religious communities cannot be treated as an ordinary consequence of conflict.
However, statements of concern must be followed by sustained diplomatic engagement and practical measures to prevent further killings.
The Ethiopian government has a fundamental responsibility to protect its citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or geographic location. That responsibility includes taking reasonable measures to prevent attacks, investigating credible reports of abuses, protecting religious institutions, and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable through fair legal proceedings.
The international community should continue pressing for these obligations to be fulfilled.

Thank you for taking the time to ask comment on my post and to share your opinions 😊💙. 

I have a different interpretation of what is happening and what will happen next. Some of the points I am about to make are already covered in the two posts I am sharing at the bottom of this post.

I don't know whether you have been following my analyses for a long time, but, in my interpretation, Sadakat is a pathological narcissist who will never change. As such, she does not genuinely love anyone, she has no empathy and has never truly loved anyone, including her children: none of them.

I agree with you that Sadakat will do everything she can to kill Ufuk and prevent Cihan from discovering the truth. However, I also believe that, as Zoya @zoya54287461698  has already suggested in the second post I am linking at the bottom, Sadakat will begin treating Kaya more favourably, without telling Cihan.

She knows perfectly well that Kaya is impulsive and that his behaviour does not offer the stability she needs. Nevertheless, I think she will start favouring him.

In my view, the main reason Sadakat chose Cihan as the family leader was not that he was Azem's son. That was a secondary consideration. The main reason was Cihan's personality and the survival mechanism he developed as a child: obedience. 

A pathological narcissist needs pawns: children, relatives, friends and anyone else who can be controlled and told what to do. If Cihan had had a temperament like Nare's or Alya's, if he had been someone who recognised injustice and openly challenged it, he would never have been chosen as the leader. Sadakat needed someone who would obey her, believe her narrative and uphold the family system.

I am actually very pleased that it has emerged that Cihan is not Sadakat's biological son, particularly because she herself did not know this. There was a widespread interpretation that Sadakat mistreated Cihan because she knew he was not her biological child. That interpretation is now disproved, and this is an important distinction.

However, I would also like Cihan not to be Azem's biological son.

There are several reasons for this. First, discovering in adulthood that the people who raised you are not your biological parents is a difficult experience. This creates an important parallel with Boran. In episode 47, Cihan insulted Boran precisely because he was Ecmel's son. Now Cihan will experience for himself what it means to discover that you were not raised by your biological parents.

There is another reason. If Cihan is not an Albora by blood, this makes his attachment to the land and the family system even more significant. When he begins questioning his own behaviour and the system he has been part of, he will understand that he is not bound to that land by blood. This gives him an additional reason, and fewer feelings of guilt, to leave. Even if he were Azem's son, he would not be obliged to remain there. But knowing that he is not Azem's biological son makes this separation even more meaningful.

There is also something else about Sadakat's behaviour towards her sons that I find particularly significant. In my interpretation, Sadakat did not genuinely try to save Cihan. She deliberately set in motion the circumstances that led to Boran's death.

My reading is that her plan was to have both sons killed. She knew that Boran was determined to kill Cihan and had already made several attempts to do so. All she needed to do was tell him where Cihan was and that he was going to marry his former wife. She knew exactly how Boran would react and deliberately pushed him towards confronting Cihan.

Boran's condition was not adequately managed or treated by the Albora family and Yalcin. Sadakat knew his state of mind and knew how dangerous he was. Her plan was to make Boran kill Cihan and then kill Boran herself.

Things did not unfold exactly as she had anticipated. If she had genuinely wanted to save Cihan, she would have acted before Boran had the opportunity to shoot him. More importantly, she would never have sent Boran into the square in those circumstances. I see this as a calculated plan, not an attempt to protect one son from the other.

Can pathological narcissistic parents deliberately kill their own children? Yes. First of all, their main aim is to drive their children to complete psychological exhaustion, subjecting them to prolonged suffering and a slow emotional and psychological decline, pushing them towards the point of losing the will to live or taking their own lives.

The crucial point is that seeing their child suffer does not make them stop, change their behaviour or show compassion. In a relationship driven by control, domination and the need to maintain power, it can, instead, become a reason to continue to use that suffering to maintain control.

They do not always need to kill their children directly. The relentless destruction of their psychological well-being can itself become a means of destroying them.

Moreover, they avoid doing so publicly because preserving their image is essential to them. Sadakat, however, has made mistakes because she is in a state of psychological regression, which is affecting her behaviour and leading her to make mistakes she would normally avoid.

I have written extensively about this psychological state (the regression mechanism) since December. It is something we have seen in Sadakat, Cihan, Alya and other characters as well.

This brings me back to Kaya who is also in regression. I think Sadakat's decision to begin favouring him without telling Cihan is particularly important.

It will allow Cihan to experience, from the other side, what it means to be treated differently within a narcissistic family. Contrary to what some viewers might think, Cihan has actually been treated better than the other children, especially Boran (and Nare). He has enjoyed many privileges that they did not have.

When Sadakat begins treating Kaya more favourably, Cihan will experience a change in the way he is treated without understanding why. This creates a very interesting parallel with Boran, who never understood why he was treated differently from Cihan. Thus, Cihan will finally experience some of the dynamics that he previously failed to recognise because he benefited from them.

text:
[The Great Data Leak Era: Why We Need a "Leak-Assumed Society," How the Rise of "Super Sapiens" Could Shake the Liberal Ideal of Equal Rights for All Conscious Beings, and the "Autoregressive Association Loop"]

[Information will leak. AI will replace human abilities. And humanity itself will change.]
I believe we need to rethink our social values based on these three assumptions.
As I kept exploring these ideas, I realized that even the one thing I thought would remain irreplaceable, my own subjective existence, raises far more difficult questions than I had imagined.

===================================
[The Great Data Leak Era Requires a "Leak-Assumed Society"]

Personal data leaks keep happening.

As AI agents automate cyberattacks, stealing information will likely become even cheaper and easier.

Smart home devices, security cameras, robot vacuum cleaners, and routers are all potential targets.

Security cameras are particularly troublesome.

Even inexpensive models allow us to check our homes remotely from a smartphone.

Many use P2P, or peer-to-peer communication.

A manufacturer's server helps establish a connection, allowing remote viewing without manually opening ports on the home router.

Because manufacturers can avoid relaying most video traffic, this approach is well suited to free services.

But if the connection management system has vulnerabilities, outsiders may gain unauthorized access to the footage.

With smaller manufacturers, there is another problem.

Can they really maintain security updates for five or ten years after selling the product?

These devices are not like traditional appliances that can simply be sold and forgotten.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[Design Cameras Assuming Someone Else Might Watch]

This led me to a different way of thinking.

[Install security cameras under the assumption that someone else might eventually see the footage.]

Point them toward entrances, driveways, and other areas where exposure would cause relatively limited harm.

Of course, even these images can reveal when someone is home.

Still, being able to check my house while I am away is an important security benefit.

I would rather preserve that convenience while reducing the potential damage.

Store recordings locally on microSD cards instead of keeping large amounts of footage in the cloud.

Automatically overwrite old recordings.

Local storage does not eliminate the risk of unauthorized access, but it reduces the danger of massive leaks from centralized cloud storage.

Celebrities and others who are particularly attractive targets may need much stronger protection.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[Individuals and Businesses Should Collect Less and Build Less]

Consumers should avoid accumulating unnecessary bank accounts, credit cards, memberships, and store-specific apps.

They should regularly check transaction histories.

Authentication should rely on reputable providers such as Google whenever appropriate, while passwords should be managed through trustworthy password managers.

Of course, signing in with Google does not protect personal information that the destination company stores independently.

Businesses need an even more fundamental change in thinking.

Customer data has traditionally been considered an asset.

But when we include security costs, breach response, legal exposure, and reputational damage, personal information becomes a [potential liability].

Do not build proprietary authentication systems without a compelling reason.

Avoid storing payment information.

Do not collect unnecessary personal data.

If a dedicated smartphone app is unnecessary, use a web app that customers can add to their home screens.

For analytics, prioritize aggregated information that cannot reasonably identify individuals.

[Alongside preventing leaks, we should build systems that simply do not possess much sensitive information to leak.]

I believe this transition toward a "Leak-Assumed Society" is becoming necessary.

===================================
[Searching for "Things Only Humans Can Do" Is a Fighting Retreat]

Every time AI improves, people search for something that supposedly belongs exclusively to humans.

Creativity belongs to humans.

Deep reasoning belongs to humans.

Empathy belongs to humans.

Human influencers can never be replaced.

But as AI acquires new abilities, these boundaries keep retreating.

Viewed from a metacognitive perspective, meaning stepping back to examine our own thinking, this is a [fighting retreat].

Why must we keep searching for humanity's final sanctuary?

I would rather start with the assumption that human abilities may eventually be replicated or surpassed by AI.

That does not mean human life loses its value.

It means separating the value of my existence from comparisons of ability.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[Even the Appeal of Celebrities Can Be Broken Down into Associations]

Consider Shohei Ohtani.

His extraordinary two-way career has repeatedly challenged conventional wisdom about baseball.

Nobody knows what he will accomplish next.

His achievements trigger associations with baseball history, past legends, expectations, and seemingly impossible records.

These associations create an unpredictable story.

And that story is exciting.

I have long been developing a hypothesis that association is a fundamental operation underlying human thought.

The appeal of celebrities may also be understood through associations triggered by their appearance, behavior, personality, and history.

If AI develops long-term memory, consistent personalities, and the ability to generate unpredictable stories through autonomous activity, virtual celebrities may eventually provide many of the same experiences.

Human sporting achievements and communities of fans will retain their own value.

But many functions traditionally provided by human celebrities may gradually be replaced.

Meanwhile, AI-powered surveillance and tracking could make fame increasingly dangerous.

[The benefits of fame may decline while its personal risks increase.]

That reversal seems entirely possible.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[The AI Business That Profits from Fear]

There is also a familiar marketing pitch.

"Learn the one secret AI can never replace."

First, create anxiety about the future.

Then offer free information.

Finally, sell expensive courses, exclusive communities, or information products.

Of course, many legitimate courses teach valuable practical skills.

The problem is selling poorly supported promises of special survival strategies by exploiting fear.

I prefer a different question.

If AI can do more and more things, what would I like to accomplish with it?

That seems far more interesting.

===================================
[Is My Own Subjective Existence the Last Irreplaceable Thing?]

I have believed that no matter how advanced AI becomes, another conscious being cannot simply experience my life in my place.

Even if an AI were created with exactly my memories and personality, our experiences would diverge from the moment of copying.

But things become more complicated if the brain is gradually replaced by artificial components.

At what point, if any, would the original subject cease to exist?

Through earlier conversations with AI, I developed what I call the [Dialogic Inner Speech = Consciousness Hypothesis].

Inner speech is the stream of words and dialogue that unfolds inside our minds.

My hypothesis is that this continuous timeline of inner speech may be a central mechanism of consciousness.

If the information processing that generates consciousness can be reproduced artificially, perhaps consciousness itself could also be copied.

However, once two copies begin receiving different sensory information, their subjective experiences diverge.

This raises another question.

[Should each copied conscious subject receive independent rights?]

And what about nonhuman subjects?

If dolphins have conscious experiences, how much moral consideration should those experiences receive?

Why should humans be entitled to decide the rights of other beings simply because we consider ourselves more intelligent?

===================================
[The Rise of "Super Sapiens" Could Shake the Ideal of Equal Rights]

This led me to an even more troubling thought experiment.

What happens if AI eventually enables extremely advanced genetic editing?

Perhaps beings could emerge with exceptional resistance to disease, dramatically extended lifespans, and intelligence far beyond that of present-day humans.

I call this hypothetical form of humanity "Super Sapiens."

Naturally, I believe any such beings should possess fundamental rights.

But what if their intelligence vastly exceeds ours?

From their perspective, the cognitive abilities of ordinary Homo sapiens might seem comparable to those of young children.

Suddenly, humans would find themselves on the [less intelligent side].

This is no joke.

If Super Sapiens came to dominate society, would they continue to respect the equal rights of Homo sapiens?

Perhaps they would say:

"You have rights, of course. But we will make the difficult decisions for you."

Even benevolent domination becomes conceivable.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[Small Genetic Changes Could Accumulate]

Modern genome editing can produce small DNA changes that might also occur naturally.

The technology is not limited to deleting DNA bases. It can also replace or insert genetic sequences.

What interests me is the possibility of accumulating many changes over generations.

First, preventing genetic diseases.

Then extending healthy lifespans.

Later, perhaps improving cognitive abilities.

Each individual improvement might seem modest.

Yet after a century, the cumulative difference could be enormous.

Of course, intelligence is a highly complex trait influenced by many genes and environmental factors.

Current technology cannot freely enhance it.

But if such capabilities eventually become possible, the boundary between Homo sapiens and Super Sapiens could become increasingly ambiguous.

A major transformation might unfold without anyone recognizing a decisive turning point.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[What If Mass Reproduction and Extreme Longevity Become Possible?]

Now imagine artificial fertilization and artificial wombs enabling dramatically higher birth rates.

What if lifespans reach 200 years, or even thousands of years?

If Super Sapiens eventually number one trillion, eight billion Homo sapiens would represent less than one percent of the population.

Under simple majority rule, ordinary humans would have almost no political influence.

I realized that respecting every existing subject equally is different from allowing unlimited creation of new subjects.

This exposed a hidden assumption in my thinking.

[Human subjects are broadly similar at the DNA level, and their reproduction is constrained by biology.]

Meanwhile, Earth's usable resources remain finite.

Modern human rights institutions developed under these conditions.

AI and genetic engineering might fundamentally change them.

We should respect the rights of conscious beings who already exist.

But how many new subjects should we be allowed to create?

How can those two principles coexist?

[Equal rights for conscious subjects are not enough, by themselves, to design a future society.]

I had underestimated the depth of this problem.

===================================
[Super Sapiens Could Merge Their Brains with AI]

There is another possibility.

Super Sapiens might not need dramatically larger brains at all.

They could connect their nervous systems directly to AI.

Imagine using additional motor nerve pathways to send commands to AI.

Additional sensory nerve pathways could receive information from AI.

What if genetic editing could produce extra nerve pathways specifically for this purpose?

Such technology does not exist today.

However, researchers are already developing prosthetic systems that read motor nerve signals and provide sensory feedback through electrical stimulation.

The next possibility is particularly interesting.

What if a child were born with neural pathways designed for AI communication?

Children learn language by listening to their parents, observing gestures, imitating sounds, and gradually predicting what comes next.

I suspect that prediction and association play central roles in this learning.

There is a broad similarity here to next-token prediction in large language models.

Perhaps a child born with neural communication pathways could learn to use them naturally through the brain's developmental plasticity, its ability to reorganize neural connections through experience.

AI could simultaneously learn to interpret the child's neural signals.

[Genes would create the communication pathways, while the brain and AI would learn to communicate together.]

Eventually, AI might become deeply integrated into the person's cognitive processes.

This would be more than an unusually intelligent human.

It could be a being capable of continuously incorporating improvements in external AI into its own cognitive abilities.

===================================
[I Am Already Thinking as "LLM Sapiens"]

I previously introduced the term "LLM Sapiens" to describe a state in which humans and AI become cognitively integrated through a shared prompt space.

I believe I am already experiencing an early form of this.

I spend hours discussing ideas with AI.

Then I ask AI to reorganize those ideas into readable articles.

I publish those articles on X.

At that point, I barely care which ideas originally came from me and which came from AI.

[If an idea is interesting, that is enough.]

I repeatedly reread our conversation history.

Each reading generates new associations.

Human reasoning and AI generation become parts of one continuous intellectual process mediated by language.

But this process remains slow.

I must type words, read responses, and interpret them.

Neurally connected Super Sapiens might eventually perform similar exchanges far more quickly.

And they could learn that communication from birth.

The resulting integration might differ in kind, not merely in speed.

===================================
[What Is the "Autoregressive Association Loop"?]

There is another interesting structure within this entire discussion.

I keep publishing extremely long posts on X.

Most receive very few impressions.

Replies are rare.

And honestly, that is fine.

Because [the most important reader is myself].

I publish my thoughts partly so that I can read them again later.

Still, there is a faint hope that someone might read them.

Perhaps someone will respond.

Perhaps an unexpected idea will come back.

That small possibility is enough to motivate me to publish.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[Publishing Encourages Information Compression]

If I am going to publish something on X, I want it to be understandable.

I could write a clear article myself if I spent enough time on it.

But I value [the speed of thinking more than the time spent polishing prose].

My own writing tends to be blunt, idiosyncratic, and sometimes difficult to follow.

So I ask AI to organize our long discussions.

Hours of conversation become a coherent, compressed article.

Then I read that article myself.

New associations emerge.

The work does not end when the article is finished.

The finished article becomes input for the next round of thinking.

I call this "Autoregressive Creation."

-----------------.-.-----------------
[X Has Become My Association Engine]

X also has a recommendation engine.

It continuously presents posts related to my interests.

Sometimes I encounter unexpected topics.

Those encounters trigger new associations.

I bring the resulting questions to AI.

Our conversation develops the ideas.

AI compresses the discussion into an article.

I publish it on X.

Then I reread it.

And the cycle begins again.

This entire discussion about a "Leak-Assumed Society" began with information about data leaks that I encountered on X.

From there, my associations moved through security cameras, corporate data management, the risks of fame, and the replacement of human abilities by AI.

Then came the rights of conscious subjects, Super Sapiens, genetic editing, and the integration of brains with AI.

I certainly did not expect the discussion to travel this far.

One association simply led to another.

-----------------.-.-----------------
[A Loop Connecting Humans, AI, and Recommendation Engines]

Each component plays a different role.

X's recommendation engine introduces new information.

I connect that information with existing ideas and discover new questions.

AI expands those questions and helps organize the reasoning.

Publishing compresses the information into a more understandable form.

I reread the result and generate new associations.

In other words, [social media is not the final destination of creative work. It is an association engine that helps generate the next thought].

Of course, recommendation algorithms can also reinforce information biases.

But their ability to introduce unexpected material remains valuable.

What I enjoy is keeping this autoregressive cycle running at high speed.

===================================
[What Matters to Me in the AI Era]

Information may leak.

Human abilities may be replaced by AI.

Genetic engineering may eventually produce conscious beings far beyond current humans.

And if those beings become an overwhelming majority, even our existing understanding of equal rights could face difficult challenges.

Initially, I believed that the one thing that would remain irreplaceable was my own subjective existence.

I still think that principle may hold.

But imagining other conscious subjects and deciding how their rights should be protected turned out to be far more complicated than I expected.

I had unconsciously assumed that the basic conditions of human society would continue indefinitely.

Even so, I have no intention of spending my life searching for abilities that AI supposedly cannot replace.

If AI becomes capable of more things, I want to use those abilities to think further.

And when an interesting idea emerges, I want to turn it into an article and read it again.

Recognition from others would be nice.

But I do not need it.

[One thought generates the next thought.]

As long as that process continues, creation never really ends for me.

And now I will probably reread this extremely long article myself.

That will trigger another association.

[The Autoregressive Association Loop]

I am already living inside it.

A Deeper Connection
It feels almost unbelievable for a mind that once had to rebuild itself from betrayal, deceit, pain, and heartache to open up again. People wander the world searching for their heart's desire or a true soulmate. I call this experience love, but it runs deeper than a simple word. It brings peace of mind, emotional clarity, and a purpose that motivates you to achieve more.
It is feeling alive once more after enduring struggles, scars, and trials, while testing how well two souls align. When a connection is meant to be, your intuition recognizes it instantly the bond is simply there, even without physical presence. It unfolds effortlessly and naturally.
When this happens, you begin viewing the world differently—letting go of past losses because they were never meant for you. It awakens parts of yourself you never knew existed or thought you had lost along the way.
When this love arrives, proceed thoughtfully. Embrace the happiness and whatever comes with it, knowing it isn't "too good to be true," but simply what was destined for you.
I found love once more amid the darkness, quieted the overwhelming thoughts, and embraced the journey. Finding love again is a true calling for those who live with intention.

You cannot truly connect with the depths of another person until you have explored the depths of your own soul. Lasting love isn't created by searching outward, but by discovering a steady inner core within yourself that remains unshakeable regardless of time, circumstance, or change.
When love originates from this place of inner peace, it recognizes the same essence in another person, making the connection feel entirely natural rather than forced. Being loved by someone who truly values themselves feels fundamentally different. It offers reassurance, safety, and ease, because you know you are being chosen out of genuine desire rather than needy dependence.
This form of love isn't about filling an internal void or escaping loneliness. It is about two complete individuals coming together from a state of wholeness, choosing each other freely, and allowing their bond to unfold without pressure, fear, or codependency.
From this foundation, love becomes a shared exchange of presence rather than a constant struggle for security. It deepens through honesty, mutual care, and the quiet recognition of something genuinely real.

Western governments are increasingly asking their populations to consider the possibility of conflict with Russia. Warnings about national resilience now sit alongside discussions of public sacrifice, wartime healthcare, and the defence of critical infrastructure. On 26 October, the defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the United Kingdom jointly identified Russia as the most acute, long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security.1

The pattern warrants attention. Several governments appear to be preparing public attitudes as well as military capabilities. Yet the available evidence supports a more qualified conclusion than a belief that war is coming: officials increasingly regard armed confrontation as a credible (as opposed to theoretical) danger that requires preparation, while continuing to assess that a major attack is neither imminent nor inevitable.

The distinction matters. Preparing for war can reflect an expectation that fighting will occur, an attempt to prevent it through deterrence, or a judgement that its consequences would be too severe to leave unaddressed. The same measure may serve all three purposes. Understanding the apparent mindset requires examining the specificity, timing, and context of official statements.

Britain offers a particularly direct example of an effort to change public expectations. In remarks reported on 15 October, General Sir Roly Walker, the head of the British Army, said political leaders would begin a “frank conversation” with citizens about danger, sacrifice, and their role in national defence. His remarks connected civilian support with the possibility that soldiers would have to fight.2

On 19 October, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting endorsed Walker’s comments in Parliament. He also described a national resilience public awareness campaign, a wider conversation about defence, and efforts to involve businesses, emergency services, and the public.3 This establishes government support for preparing society mentally. It does not establish that ministers have privately concluded that war is probable.

France has similarly placed national attitudes within its defence planning. Its July 2025 strategic review identified open war in the heart of Europe as the principal threat through 2030 and called for the country to be materially and morally prepared for a major conflict. The document resulted from work involving multiple ministries, rather than an isolated military speech.4

In November 2025, France’s chief of defence, General Fabien Mandon, explained his warning of a possible confrontation within three to four years. He linked the urgency to the pattern of Russian aggression and to the possibility that Moscow would perceive an opportunity in Europe.5 Such reasoning comes closer to anticipating a future military challenge than merely acknowledging that war is theoretically possible. Nevertheless, a possible confrontation remains different from a forecast that one will occur.

German intelligence officials have also described an increasingly concrete threat. At a parliamentary hearing on 5 October 2026, BND President Martin Jäger warned that Germany was in danger of entering a violent conflict with Russia. Military intelligence chief Martina Rosenberg contrasted earlier abstract threats with concrete attacks against Germany.6 The immediate context included sabotage and covert violence, so these remarks should not be treated as an unqualified prediction of conventional war.

Civilian planning provides another indicator. In May, Norway instructed health authorities to prepare plans for making 7,000 beds available for civilian and military war casualties. The government described this as a planning estimate; the beds would become available through wartime adaptation of the health service.7 In October, Swedish authorities announced geographically specific healthcare planning for war, including emergency hospitals based on existing provision in northern Sweden.8

These measures show that governments are considering how their societies would function under wartime conditions. Their evidential value lies in the involvement of civilian institutions and the specificity of the requirements. They reveal a serious planning assumption, although they cannot by themselves establish how likely officials believe war to be.

The most significant recent warning about a nearer-term military confrontation came from Denmark. On 24 September, its defence intelligence service assessed a low but growing risk of limited Russian military attacks against NATO countries bordering Russia. Such attacks, it said, could potentially occur within months, even while the Ukraine war continued and without Russia possessing the capability for a larger regional war.9

This identifies a potential route into hostilities that does not depend on preparations for a full-scale invasion. A limited strike, incursion, or miscalculation could create a dangerous confrontation before either side had decided to fight a general war. Denmark’s assessment therefore deserves attention, including its explicit qualification that the risk remains low.

There are, however, substantial reasons to avoid reading every preparedness campaign as evidence that governments anticipate fighting.

Maintaining emergency plans is a normal responsibility of government. The European Union’s preparedness programme encompasses natural disasters, health emergencies, infrastructure disruption, and security threats. Its guidance on household self-sufficiency for at least 72 hours addresses that wider range of risks.10 Emergency supplies are useful across several scenarios, so advice to obtain them is a weak indicator of an expectation of war specifically.

Historical context matters as well. Sweden’s crisis-and-war brochure has predecessors dating back decades, including an edition distributed in 2018. Its current guidance explicitly seeks to increase public understanding of the seriousness of the security situation, but the practice itself predates the latest warnings.11 Renewed emphasis can signal rising concern without indicating a newly discovered threat of imminent attack.

Military readiness deadlines also require careful interpretation. In April 2026, Germany’s General Carsten Breuer explained the assessment that Russia could possess the capability for a large-scale attack on NATO territory from 2029. He explicitly cautioned that this did not mean an attack would automatically happen.12 A date for potential capability is not a date for an expected decision to use it.

Actual deployments can likewise have several explanations. NATO describes activities such as Baltic Sentry and Eastern Sentry as responses to threats against infrastructure and violations of allied airspace. They strengthen surveillance, protection, and deterrence.13 Such movements substantiate the seriousness of the security environment, but they can be intended to keep a confrontation contained.

On the other hand, as we have seen recently, military preparations for attack can be hidden in what are described as “routine” and “defensive” movements.

The severity of the possible consequences further complicates the inference. Governments may devote substantial resources to preventing a catastrophe they still consider unlikely. Preparation demonstrates that a risk has crossed a threshold for action; it does not necessarily demonstrate that the event has become the expected outcome. Conversely, the absence of mobilisation would not prove that officials were unconcerned.

Current official assessments also contain affirmative evidence against an expectation of imminent major war.

On 14 October, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance saw no imminent threat against its territory. Estonia’s Foreign Ministry separately reported that there were no Russian forces or other signs of preparations for an imminent military confrontation at NATO’s borders.14 These statements concern observable preparations, making them more specific than general expressions of confidence.

Estonia’s defence minister had also responded directly to Denmark’s September warning. After a recent intelligence update, he said the threat did not require an increase in armed-forces readiness and emphasised that Russia’s main effort remained focused on Ukraine.15 This illustrates why a warning from one allied government should not automatically be interpreted as a shared expectation of impending war.

Britain’s MI5 director offered a further qualification on 13 October. He described Russian hostile activity as escalating while remaining deliberately below the threshold for NATO collective defence.16 That assessment suggests Moscow is seeking to cause harm while avoiding conventional conflict. It does not eliminate the risk of escalation through error, but it weighs against treating every hostile act as a step in a settled plan for general war.

Norway’s hospital announcement illustrates how preparation and reassurance can coexist. In the same statement that required wartime casualty planning, Defence Minister Tore O. Sandvik said war affecting Norway in the near future was not considered likely.7 Denmark, despite its warning about limited attacks, likewise reported no indications of an outright invasion and assessed that prospect as highly unlikely.9

The United States’ public intelligence assessment places particular emphasis on the danger of an escalatory spiral leading to direct hostilities with Russia.17 That is a serious concern, but it describes a pathway by which conflict could develop rather than a prediction that a Russian attack on NATO is approaching.

Public assurances cannot settle what governments privately believe. Officials have reasons to preserve confidence and avoid unnecessary alarm. But assuming that every reassurance conceals the opposite judgement would make the hypothesis impossible to test. Warnings and reassurances should both be assessed against their specificity, their consistency with other evidence, and the period they address.

The strongest interpretation of the overall pattern is that several European governments have moved beyond treating war with Russia as a remote contingency. They are preparing populations for a prolonged confrontation in which direct fighting is a credible possibility. Some senior officials appear to anticipate a future military test unless deterrence improves. Evidence of a shared Western conclusion that war will probably happen remains insufficient.

Further indications of such a shift could emerge before overt mobilisation: shortened civilian preparation deadlines, more specific assessments of Russian intent, and independent agreement among intelligence agencies and political leaders about a near-term scenario. Repeated speeches drawing on the same underlying assessment would carry less weight than corroboration from separate sources.

The public has reason to take the warnings seriously and to follow practical preparedness advice. The present evidence supports warning of a substantive danger and deliberate efforts to prepare societies for it. It does not support presenting war as an outcome governments have already accepted as probable, or as an imminent event they are concealing.

Be informed. Be Prepared. Be Safe.

This is The DEFCON Warning System.

text:
The Empire were the good guys. At minimum, the Jedi were the bad ones, and it isn't close.

The original trilogy runs on Saturday-morning-cartoon morality: space wizards good, planet-killer bad. Then Lucas came back as an older man to explain why the most gifted Jedi alive would walk away. In doing so he accidentally made three movies of evidence for the defense.

Exhibit A: the Republic. Its Senate was too paralyzed to stop a trade blockade of one of its own worlds, and nothing passed until every faction got its cut. The Jedi spent those years running errands for it like galactic rent-a-cops. Meanwhile a Sith Lord climbed to the top of the government they were supposed to be guarding. No wonder Anakin, told his politics sounded like a dictatorship, shrugged: "Well, if it works."

Exhibit B: how they treated him. He was a boy conceived by the Force, the Chosen One of their own prophecy, and the Council didn't want him, mostly because he scared them. Qui-Gon won him in a bet and left his mother in slavery. In ten years the Order never went back for her. They forbade him to marry, under a code that treats love as a character flaw. They gave him a Council seat, denied him the rank of Master in the same breath, then asked him to spy on the Chancellor. When he came to Yoda terrified of losing someone, the advice was to let go of everything he feared to lose. He came back from Tatooine having done something unspeakable, and his teachers never even noticed.

Exhibit C: the Code. It was sacred every time it cost Anakin something. The moment it protected Palpatine (disarmed, beaten, owed a trial), Mace Windu decided he was too dangerous to live. This was the same Mace who had floated the idea of the Council taking control of the Senate. They threw the Code out the window the second it suited them, which is how Mace ended up out the window himself.

Exhibit D: everything else. "Only a Sith deals in absolutes" is an absolute. They took babies from their parents. They were peacekeepers who led a cloned army they never ordered and never questioned. They revered the prophecy until it got inconvenient, then decided it had been misread. Their plan to finish the Sith was to send a son to kill his father. Luke refused, and what actually saved the galaxy was the attachment the Jedi spent generations forbidding. Even Luke ended up calling their legacy failure and hypocrisy.

Anakin wanted what a lot of young men want: a wife, a family, a chance to be a hero and fix what was broken. The Republic offered him celibacy, suspicion, and errands. Palpatine offered a way to save the woman he loved. That's why this story hits so hard for so many young guys. The tragedy isn't that Anakin got corrupted. It's that he chased the things they want too, and lost everything anyway.

Not that anyone wins. Vader becomes a cyborg and Palpatine a cryptkeeper. Obi-Wan spends nearly twenty years in a desert hut, and Luke follows the Jedi path to an island where he drinks green milk from a sea monster. The New Republic inherits every problem the old one had. https://t.co/6r1zcb06gH

In other words, the implication is that Russia somehow stands apart from all of this—that it never waged war, never engaged in plunder, and, as it were, had nothing to do with it. Or so it might seem. But that is not the case. Let’s simply ask Google, and it provides the answer: Since 1700, Russia (in its various incarnations—the Russian Empire, the USSR, and the Russian Federation) has participated in dozens of major armed conflicts. In historical scholarship and international law, the classification of these wars as "wars of conquest," "colonial" wars, or "wars of liberation" depends on the methodology used; assessments of the very same conflict can vary radically depending on national historiography and the political perspectives of the parties involved.
Below is a list of major wars, along with the approaches used in global and Russian scholarship to classify them, as well as the status of conflicts that took place during the Cold War. Major Wars of Russia (Since 1700) and Their Classification

Historians often categorize these conflicts based on their primary geopolitical objectives:

1. Wars of Conquest, Expansion, and Colonization

In global historiography (as well as, to some extent, in Soviet and Russian historiography), this category encompasses conflicts aimed at territorial expansion, the subjugation of other peoples, or the maintenance of control over dependent regions:
• The Partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1772, 1793, 1795): These led to the dissolution of the Polish-Lithuanian state and the division of its territories among Russia, Prussia, and Austria.
• ​​The Caucasian War (1817–1864): A classic example of a colonial war, involving the subjugation of the highland peoples of the North Caucasus and the incorporation of the region into the Russian Empire.
• The Conquest of Central Asia (19th century): Military campaigns against the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanates of Khiva and Kokand, driven by imperial expansion and rivalry with Great Britain (the "Great Game").
• The Soviet-Finnish War (1939–1940): Initiated by the USSR with the goal of pushing the border further away from Leningrad; it was recognized by the international community (the League of Nations) as an act of aggression.
• The Suppression of Uprisings and Revolutions (Interventions): This includes the crushing of Polish uprisings (1830, 1863) and the Hungarian Revolution (1849), as well as the deployment of troops into Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968) to maintain control over spheres of influence. 2. Just, Defensive, and Liberation Wars

This category includes wars initiated in response to external aggression, for the purpose of defending sovereignty, ensuring the survival of the state, or liberating territories from occupation:
• The Patriotic War of 1812: A defensive war against the invasion by Napoleon’s army.
• The Great Patriotic War (1941–1945): A just war of liberation waged by the Soviet people against Nazi Germany and its allies, fought for the survival of the state and the elimination of the threat of genocide.

The Évian outcome functions as a specific judgment on Ashkenazi Jews rather than a mechanical result of generic constraints.

Delegates cited unemployment, saturation, and existing quotas, yet those factors did not produce equivalent coordinated refusals for other European groups. Australia’s representative stated directly that the country had “no real racial problem” and was “not desirous of importing one.” Several Latin American delegations specified preferences against merchants and intellectuals—standard coded language for urban Ashkenazi professionals—and some required Christian baptism or intermarriage conditions. The conference was convened explicitly for German and Austrian Jews; no parallel meeting was held to decide the fate of Sudeten Germans, Spanish Republicans, or other White European refugee streams under the same Depression conditions.

The Johnson-Reed quotas existed and were not waived. The United States treated them as ceilings rather than floors; large numbers of German quota slots went unfilled between 1933 and 1941. Britain limited Palestine. France declared saturation. These were legal and political choices, not immutable barriers. When political will existed for other categories—limited Australian intake, the Dominican Republic’s large offer under Trujillo, or earlier acceptance of White Russian refugees—legal pathways were found or created. The near-unanimous non-offer of substantial new numbers for this particular group, combined with explicit racial language from multiple delegations, tracks the ethnicity of the refugees more closely than the shared background conditions of the 1930s.

The data therefore support treating the conference result as a broad, multi-national assessment of the group itself.

🛸 Story time - A Florida company offers insurance for alien abduction.
And yes, people actually bought it.

Here is the full story:

In 1987, a Florida insurance man named Mike St. Lawrence was watching Larry King interview Whitley Strieber, the author of a book about alien encounters. He checked his own homeowner's policy and found it did not cover alien abduction. So he wrote a policy that did.

His agency, the St. Lawrence Agency in Altamonte Springs, Florida, has sold it ever since. The classic price is $19.95 for lifetime cover, with a headline of $10 million. The catch is the payout: $1 a year. At that rate, collecting the full $10 million would take 10 million years.

The fine print is where the jokes live. The policy includes psychiatric care, "sarcasm coverage" for the heckling you get from family, and double identity coverage. Payout doubles if the alien insists on conjugal visits or refers to you as a nutritional food source.

To claim, you need proof, normally the signature of an authorized onboard alien. St. Lawrence says he has made exceptions and paid out one or two claims, $1 a year, including one claimant he says sent him $1 in a Christmas card each year until he lost the address. Those claim stories come from him, not from an independent check.

By his own count, repeated by local TV news, he has sold roughly 6,000 policies. The Florida Department of Insurance noticed and let sales continue. The "UFO Abduction Insurance" banner in the 1997 film Contact was his real banner, not a movie prop.

The bottom line, and the explainer moral: it is a real business selling a real piece of paper, but by the seller's own word it is a novelty. The headline number means nothing until you read how it pays out.

I finally took the time to analyze $TSLA Q3'26 earnings call. 

While we are all aware of the reasons for why $TSLA won't skyrocket higher from here and instead go lower, there are some arguments to be made on why it could break past resistance and go higher.

First, the Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown by a factor of 10 since launching last month. Tesla has been rapidly deploying CyberCabs in Texas, and eventually, the Tesla team will make the robotaxi business have 24/7 operations and cover more weather/high-speed conditions by the end of the year.

Plus, Elon even noted that they have a clear path to their target of $0.30 per paid mile because they own the vehicle manufacturing and have no driver costs. They'll get there eventually, not now. 

Secondly, Optimus began production in the Fremont factory, and management expects to deliver Optimus to companies outside Tesla around Q4 2027.

A non-pre-programmed, real-world AI demo video is expected in 1-2 months, and that will boost investor confident into Optimus becoming a sales catalyst in the near future. 

In terms of their bread-and-butter automotive business, Elon noted that over 75% of deliveries in North America included a paid FSD subscription, with over 1.7 million paid customers globally, and half of them are on the subscription plan.

Management confirmed investor estimates that FSD Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) is approaching $1 billion.

Unsupervised FSD is expected to roll out in Q2'27, and with that rollout, they'll let customers release their vehicles into the robotaxi network so that owners can get a piece of the profits that are to be made in the growing robotaxi business.

In ways, this move helps them offer lower prices, as many Tesla customers who would put their vehicles into the robotaxi network would happily take any money from servicing a ride rather than let their vehicle bake in the sun. 

Tesla is currently having its highest backlog in 4 years and is doing everything it can to produce more vehicles. The high gas prices have helped a lot with boosting demand for Tesla vehicles, and the price hikes have boosted their automotive gross margins from 16% to 18%. 

By 2030, Tesla hopes to produce 5 million vehicles annually. Factories are already operating at record rates, and Tesla will open more factories in the future.

In terms of energy, Tesla almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027. The average selling price and margins on Megapacks will grow due to the insane demand for batteries thanks to the AI buildout.

Terrafab, which will be key to Tesla's new chapter, will see its first test chip be produced in May/June 2027, with volume production looking to start in Q3 2028. 

Financially, Tesla is solid with $45B in cash and over $1.5B in FCF during Q3'26. While they revised CapEx spending projections for 2026, next year and the year after will have higher CapEx spending due to the Terafab, robotaxi expansion, Optimus production, and buying more Nvidia GPUs. 

One can argue that robotaxis and a sold-out auto and energy business make for a great bull case for $TSLA. But I think that once they are in the final phases of their CapEx spending and the investments will start bearing fruit, that's when Tesla will truly go on another generational run sometime in 2028. 

Other than that, let's enjoy the opportunity we have in accumulating more shares of an innovative business with a bright future.
